one_liner: GROQ query linter whose 13 pure-GROQ rules run in a Rust-to-WASM build; claims 5-10x over its own TypeScript rules, with no measurement.
what_it_does: A pnpm monorepo of linting tools for Sanity GROQ queries and schemas: an ESLint plugin, a CLI (@sanity-labs/groq-lint), an LSP server, a Prettier plugin, and @sanity-labs/groq-wasm, which wraps atombender's Rust groq-lint and groq-format crates through wasm-bindgen. @sanity-labs/groq-lint's lint(query, {config, schema, forceTs}) sends the 13 pure-GROQ rules to WASM automatically and runs the remaining rules (deep-pagination-param and the schema-aware invalid-type-filter and unknown-field) in TypeScript on a groq-js AST. groq-wasm can also be used on its own: lint(query) returns findings, format(query, {width}) formats.
how_it_is_fast: The pure-GROQ rules move from TypeScript AST walks over groq-js to a Rust pipeline: the groq-parser-rs parser lowers the AST to an IR, and 14 rule passes check it in one call. Findings cross the boundary once, as a JSON string. The WASM module is built by wasm-pack with opt-level 's' (size) and LTO, and loaded synchronously at import. Nothing in the repo measures the effect.
when_to_use: You already lint GROQ with the Sanity ESLint plugin, CLI or LSP; the WASM path comes with @sanity-labs/groq-lint and costs nothing to adopt
Linting large batches of GROQ queries in CI or an editor, where the Rust rule passes may beat the TypeScript walks (unmeasured)
Browser or edge use where you want GROQ formatting (groq-format) without a Rust toolchain
Node.js 22.3.0 or newer with ESM, which both packages require
when_not_to_use: If you need a proven speedup: the '~5-10x faster' line has no benchmark, corpus, runtime version or hardware behind it, and the repo has no bench script
When findings must be identical across paths: WASM findings keep the Rust severities and rule semantics, which differ from the TypeScript rules they replace
Schema-aware linting: invalid-type-filter and unknown-field always run in TypeScript on a groq-js parse, so a WASM run parses each query twice
Older Node.js or CommonJS-only toolchains: 1.0.0 dropped CJS builds and requires Node.js 22.3.0 or newer
Stability-sensitive production use: Sanity Labs calls it 'pre-v1' and maintained on a 'best-effort basis'; 7 stars, and upstream rule logic is regenerated by an LLM from rules.yaml

integration.form: module (npm ESM packages with a prebuilt wasm-pack binary; Node entry plus browser entry)
integration.dependencies: @sanity-labs/groq-wasm: none at runtime (bundled .wasm). @sanity-labs/groq-lint: groq-js, @sanity/codegen, @sanity-labs/lint-core, @sanity-labs/groq-wasm. Rebuilding the WASM needs Rust, the wasm32-unknown-unknown target and wasm-pack; the Rust crate pins atombender/groq-lint dd5e8fb, atombender/groq-format 2b43ee9 and sanity-io/groq-parser-rs 82e343c through Cargo.lock
integration.min_toolchain: Node.js >= 22.3.0 (engines field; CHANGELOG 1.0.0); pnpm >= 9 for development; Rust toolchain version not documented
integration.platforms: any platform with WebAssembly: Node.js (WASM read with readFileSync and initSync at import) and modern browsers (browser entry)
integration.thread_safety: not documented; calls are synchronous on the JS thread
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — @sanity-labs/groq-lint uses WASM automatically for its 13 rules (forceTs: true turns it off), but severities and some rule behaviour differ from the TypeScript rules, and standalone groq-wasm returns Rust severities and byte-offset spans

gotchas: The default lint() call still parses every query with groq-js. deep-pagination-param is not in WASM_RULES and needs no schema, so it always runs in TypeScript, even though its own source comment says groq-js 'does not support parameters in slice expressions', so it can never fire. A default call therefore pays the groq-js parse plus a Rust parse, IR lowering and a JSON round trip. The claimed 5-10x can apply at most to the WASM call measured on its own, never to the end-to-end lint(). Disabling deep-pagination-param (with no schema) is the only way to skip the groq-js parse.

Severities differ between paths. computed-value-in-filter is 'warning' in the TypeScript rule but 'high' in upstream rules.yaml, which mapSeverity turns into 'error'. Setting forceTs, or the per-query fallback that runs when the Rust parser throws, therefore changes what CI fails on. The Rust linter also runs deep_pagination_param, whose findings are filtered out.

Wrong source positions after non-ASCII text. byteOffsetToLocation in packages/groq-wasm/src/lint.ts advances its counter by one per code point, while the WASM returns UTF-8 byte offsets. Line and column numbers therefore drift for any finding that follows a non-ASCII character, and the 'offset' field it returns is a byte offset, not a JS string index.

The docs are stale. packages/groq-wasm/README.md still documents initWasm, isInitialized, lintAsync and formatAsync, and packages/groq-lint/README.md still documents initLinter(); CHANGELOG 1.0.0 removed all of them. Since 1.0.0 the WASM loads at import time and a load failure throws WasmError. The root README's 'automatic fallback to TypeScript if WASM unavailable' therefore no longer covers load failures, only queries the Rust parser rejects.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: No sibling lints GROQ, so this is the only choice for that job. Unlike sh-syntax, es-module-lexer or hash-wasm, which publish measured WASM-versus-JS numbers, this entry's speedup is an unbenchmarked README ratio; treat it as a convenience of the Sanity lint toolchain, not as a proven fast path.
verified_claims_summary: First-party README text only. The root README says pure GROQ rules run via Rust/WASM '~5-10x faster', and packages/groq-wasm/README.md says '~5-10x faster than TypeScript for complex queries'. No benchmark code, query corpus, Node.js or browser version, hardware or sample count exists in the repo. In the default lint() path the TypeScript groq-js parse still runs, so the end-to-end gain must be smaller than any ratio for the WASM call alone.
status_note: Active (last commit 2026-09-25, packages at 1.0.0, MIT, 7 stars, 2 open issues) but 'pre-v1' and best-effort by its own description. Easy to adopt inside the Sanity lint toolchain; the speed claim is unmeasured, and the default path keeps the TypeScript parse it claims to replace.
